Debt Crisis Hits India’s Diversified Industrials Sector as Firms Struggle to Refinance

India’s diversified industrials sector is facing its worst financial turmoil in over a decade as a mounting debt crisis squeezes the liquidity and credit lines of major players across the country. The ongoing crisis, triggered by a combination of rising interest rates and a sudden withdrawal of short-term credit by key lenders, has left several firms in the sector unable to meet their financial obligations, prompting fears of large-scale layoffs and plant closures.

At the center of the crisis is the rapid deterioration in credit availability that began in late May, when several non-banking financial institutions abruptly tightened lending standards for industrial conglomerates. According to the Federation of Indian Diversified Industries (FIDI), at least 37% of firms in the sector are now “at risk of default” on existing loans, with some facing immediate insolvency.

“Many of our members are reporting severe cash flow shortages, and the situation is getting worse by the day,” said Prakash Sethi, President of FIDI. “We are urging policymakers and financial institutions to urgently intervene before there is irreversible damage to the sector’s productive capacity.”

Several large plant sites have either reduced operations or halted production altogether in recent days. In Gujarat, workers at the Laxmi Multiproduct Complex reported that three of the facility’s five divisions have been temporarily shut due to a lack of working capital. “We were told to go on unpaid leave until further notice,” said Anil Sharma, a technician at the site. “There is no clarity on when we can return.”

The impact is being felt across India’s major industrial corridors, from Maharashtra to Tamil Nadu. A senior executive at Suryodaya Holdings, a leading conglomerate in the sector, confirmed that the company is “reviewing all capital expenditure and considering asset sales” as debt repayments loom.

Industry analysts warn that without prompt relief, the crisis may deepen further. “If this credit freeze persists, we could see a wave of bankruptcies in the coming weeks,” said Rekha Jindal, Senior Analyst at TrustEdge Ratings. “The ripple effects on employment and site utilization are already significant.”

With the crisis ongoing and uncertainty prevailing, union leaders have called for immediate talks with management and government representatives. “Thousands of livelihoods are at stake,” said Rakesh Kumar, Secretary of the All India Industrial Workers Union. “We need a concrete plan to safeguard jobs and restart operations.”
